title: VA Denied Your Disability Claim Despite a Favorable C&P Exam: How to Appeal
excerpt: What to do when VA denies a claim despite a favorable C&P medical opinion, including evidence review, legal errors, and appeal options.
body:
A favorable Compensation and Pension examination can be important evidence, but it does not guarantee an award. VA may deny a claim because another required element is missing, because it finds competing evidence more persuasive, or because it made a factual or legal error. The next step is to determine which happened.

A Favorable Opinion Is Evidence, Not the Final Decision

A C&P examiner may conclude that a condition is at least as likely as not related to service. The adjudicator still determines whether the legal elements of entitlement are satisfied. For example, the record may contain a dispute about qualifying service, the diagnosis, or the factual premise of the opinion.

A decision should explain how material evidence was considered. An unsupported dismissal of a favorable opinion can provide a focused basis for review.

Compare the Examiner’s Findings With the Rating Decision

Read the full medical opinion, not just the summary checkbox. Identify what records the examiner reviewed, the diagnosis, the nexus conclusion, and the rationale. Then read the VA decision’s reasons and bases and favorable findings.

Sometimes the rating decision appears to describe an opinion as negative even though its actual conclusion is favorable. In other cases, the examiner offers a favorable statement that is contradicted by the stated rationale. The distinction matters.

Common Reasons for an Apparently Contradictory Denial

VA may rely on another opinion, question the factual history used by the examiner, or determine that an element of the claim is missing. It may also fail to address relevant lay evidence, overlook an alternative theory, or use an inadequate medical opinion.

The best appeal argument identifies a specific contradiction or omission. Simply saying “my exam was favorable” does not tell the reviewer why the denial was legally wrong.

How to Choose an Appeal Option

Higher-Level Review can be appropriate when the existing record already shows an error. A Supplemental Claim is designed for new and relevant evidence. Board appeal options have different evidentiary rules and timelines.

For many decisions, filing the proper review within one year can preserve continuous pursuit. Read the decision notice before choosing a lane.

When a New Medical Opinion Helps

If VA’s denial exposes an unresolved medical question, a carefully reasoned private nexus opinion may address it. But if the record already contains a sufficient favorable opinion and VA simply misread it, adding more medical evidence may not be the most efficient first step.

A good appeal strategy starts with the decision and the existing evidence, then determines what, if anything, is actually missing.

What to Do Before Filing or Appealing

A favorable examination should be analyzed alongside the full record and VA’s stated reasons. The strongest challenge is precise, evidence-based, and tailored to the actual error.

Keep the rating decision and notification letter, identify the exact issue under dispute, collect the relevant records, and review the deadline before selecting a review option. Evidence that answers VA’s specific reason for denial is more useful than a stack of unrelated documents.

title: VA Denied Your Claim for Lack of Medical Nexus: What Next?
excerpt: A current diagnosis and an in-service event do not always establish service connection. Learn how to identify the missing medical link and respond strategically.
body:
A current diagnosis and an in-service event do not always establish service connection. Learn how to identify the missing medical link and respond strategically. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

What a medical nexus actually establishes

For many direct service-connection claims, VA must find a current disability, a qualifying in-service disease, injury, or event, and a relationship between the two. That relationship is often called the medical nexus. A veteran may have extensive treatment records proving the current diagnosis and still be denied if the evidence does not connect it to service.

Read the favorable findings before responding. If VA already conceded the current disability and an in-service event, the dispute may be much narrower than the denial letter initially suggests.

Why a bare conclusion is weak evidence

An opinion stating only that a condition 'is at least as likely as not related to service' may be less persuasive if it does not explain why. A useful opinion identifies the relevant medical facts, onset and course of symptoms, exposure or injury, applicable medical principles, and why alternative explanations are more or less likely.

A clinician need not use magic words to be persuasive. What matters is whether the reasoning permits the adjudicator to understand the conclusion and evaluate it against contrary evidence.

Review the VA examiner’s factual assumptions

Some negative opinions rest on an assertion that no relevant event occurred, no symptoms were reported, or no treatment happened for many years. Compare those assertions against the actual service records, personnel history, lay statements, and post-service records. An opinion built on a materially inaccurate factual premise may have reduced probative value.

A gap in treatment can be relevant, but it is not automatically dispositive. The examiner should consider competent reports of symptoms and explain their medical significance rather than substitute silence in the records for a complete analysis.

Practical takeaway: Before choosing a review option or submitting more evidence, compare the rating decision with the records VA actually considered. The most useful next step addresses the precise missing legal or factual element.

Choose the review lane that matches the deficiency

If the examiner ignored evidence already in the record or VA failed to obtain a necessary opinion, a Higher-Level Review may be appropriate to identify an error based on the prior record. If the claim genuinely needs a new medical nexus opinion, a Supplemental Claim with new and relevant evidence may be more effective. The two approaches solve different problems.

Preserve applicable one-year review deadlines when possible. A late Supplemental Claim can still be available, but the potential effective date may change.

Direct, secondary, and presumptive theories differ

A nexus dispute can arise under direct service connection, secondary service connection, or a presumptive theory. Under 38 C.F.R. § 3.310, a secondary opinion may need to address both causation and aggravation. For a qualifying presumptive condition, the law may supply the connection when the required service and diagnosis criteria are met. Do not demand a traditional nexus opinion for a presumption that removes that requirement.

The correct theory depends on the veteran's service, diagnosis, and evidence. Multiple theories may be reasonably raised, but each should be analyzed on its own terms.

Build the record around the denied element

A focused submission can include a detailed chronology, medical records, competent lay statements, deployment or personnel documentation, and a well-reasoned opinion addressing the prior denial. Ask the clinician to review the specific unfavorable examination and explain any disagreement with its factual or medical assumptions.

More paperwork is not automatically better evidence. The objective is to resolve the precise uncertainty that caused the denial while keeping the procedural history and effective date intact.

Questions to ask before you file

  • What exactly did VA concede in its favorable findings, and what element remains disputed?
  • Which evidence was already in the record when VA made the decision?
  • Is the issue a legal or factual mistake, missing development, or a genuine lack of supporting evidence?
  • What is the date of the decision notice, and which review deadline applies?
  • Would the proposed evidence answer the specific reason VA gave for its decision?

title: VA Denied Your PACT Act Claim: What Should You Do Next?
excerpt: A practical guide to appealing denied PACT Act VA claims, identifying mistakes in presumptive service connection, and protecting appeal deadlines.
body:
A denial labeled “PACT Act” can mean several different things. VA may dispute the veteran’s qualifying service, the diagnosis, the relationship to exposure, or the claimed rating. Before filing another form, identify which element VA says is missing.

Read the Favorable Findings First

Modern VA decisions often list favorable findings. These can include a current diagnosis, a conceded toxic exposure risk activity, or qualifying service. Under the applicable rules, favorable findings are generally binding on later VA adjudicators unless properly rebutted.

A denial may concede exposure but reject service connection because the diagnosed condition is not presumptive. That is a different problem from a decision that incorrectly states the veteran never served in a covered location.

Confirm the Diagnosis Matches the Law

The PACT Act identifies specific diseases and covered service circumstances. A symptom such as chronic coughing is not necessarily the same as a documented diagnosis of asthma, chronic bronchitis, or another listed disease.

Review the exact medical terminology, diagnostic testing, and whether VA considered the condition actually claimed. Where a diagnosis is disputed, updated clinical evidence may be necessary.

Check Deployment Dates and Locations

VA can make factual mistakes about service dates, temporary duty, or locations. Deployment orders, personnel records, unit records, and other official evidence can establish qualifying service.

A veteran should not assume that a denial is correct merely because the DD214 lacks a detailed list of every location visited.

Choose the Right Review Lane

Higher-Level Review generally uses the existing evidentiary record and can address factual or legal errors. A Supplemental Claim permits new and relevant evidence. A Board appeal offers different docket options with distinct evidence rules.

For most VA decisions, filing an appropriate review request within one year is important to preserve continuous pursuit and potential effective-date rights. Different deadlines and exceptions can apply, so read the actual notice.

What If the Disease Is Not Presumptive

VA still must consider a properly raised direct service-connection theory when supported by the record. A competent medical opinion can address exposure history, disease development, alternative causes, and the individual veteran’s circumstances.

The correct argument is not that the PACT Act automatically covers every illness. It is that the law’s presumption, if applicable, or the evidence supporting direct service connection must be analyzed correctly.

What to Do Before Filing or Appealing

A targeted appeal can be more effective than simply submitting the same diagnosis and the same statement again without addressing VA’s stated reason for denial.

Keep the rating decision and notification letter, identify the exact issue under dispute, collect the relevant records, and review the deadline before selecting a review option. Evidence that answers VA’s specific reason for denial is more useful than a stack of unrelated documents.

title: How VA Combined Ratings Work , And Why the Math Usually Shortchanges Veterans
excerpt: Most veterans assume their disability percentages simply add together. The VA’s “whole person” method produces a lower number in almost every case , understanding it is the first step to knowing whether your rating is correct.
body:
The Myth of Simple Addition

Ask most veterans how the VA calculates a combined disability rating and they’ll say the same thing: you add them up. A 50% rating plus a 30% rating equals 80%, right? Wrong. The VA uses a mathematical method called the “whole person” approach, and it almost always produces a combined rating that is meaningfully lower than simple addition would suggest.

This isn’t a bug in the system , it’s the intended design. The theory is that each subsequent disability affects a person who is already diminished by the previous one, so the percentages are applied sequentially to a shrinking remainder rather than stacked on top of each other.

How the Whole Person Method Works

The VA treats a healthy veteran as a whole person, represented as 100%. The first and highest-rated disability is applied to that whole person. Whatever percentage remains becomes the baseline for the next calculation. Each subsequent condition is then rated against the remaining, not the original 100%.

Step by step, the process looks like this:

  • Start with 100% (the whole, healthy person)
  • Apply the highest-rated disability. A 50% rating means 50% of the person is now impaired, leaving 50% of the person intact
  • Apply the next disability to the remaining 50%. A 30% rating against the remaining 50% adds 15% of impairment to the total
  • That produces a combined value of 65%, which then rounds to the nearest 10% , in this case, 70%

Key rule: The VA always applies ratings highest-to-lowest and rounds the final combined value to the nearest 10%. A combined value ending in 5 or higher rounds up; 4 or lower rounds down.

A Real-World Example

Suppose a veteran has three service-connected conditions rated at 70%, 50%, and 30%. Here’s how the math plays out under the whole person method:

  • Start: 100% whole person
  • Apply 70%: 70% impaired, 30% remains
  • Apply 50% to remaining 30%: 50% × 30 = 15% additional impairment. Running total: 85%
  • Apply 30% to remaining 15%: 30% × 15 = 4.5% additional impairment. Running total: 89.5%
  • Round to nearest 10%: 90%

Simple addition of 70 + 50 + 30 would suggest 150% , obviously impossible , but even capping that at 100%, the intuitive expectation of 100% is very different from the 90% the veteran actually receives. With less severe disabilities, the gap between expectation and reality is even larger.

The Bilateral Factor

One adjustment that works in veterans’ favor is the bilateral factor. If a veteran has service-connected disabilities affecting both arms, both legs, or a paired combination (e.g., one arm and one leg), the VA adds a 10% bonus to the combined value of those bilateral disabilities before applying the whole person method to the rest of the rating. This is an exception worth knowing , it can meaningfully increase a combined rating for veterans with paired extremity conditions.

Why This Matters for Your Claim

Understanding combined ratings is important at two points in the claims process. First, it explains why getting every eligible condition service-connected matters , each additional condition, even a lower-rated one, continues to push the combined rating upward, even if only incrementally. Second, it reveals why the ordering of ratings and the accuracy of each individual percentage affects the outcome. A condition that is underrated pulls down the combined rating more than it might appear to.

The point at which combined ratings are most consequential is at the 100% threshold and at the 70% threshold (which is the minimum for certain TDIU claims). Veterans who are close to either of those figures should pay careful attention to whether each individual condition has been rated accurately.

What to Do If Your Rating Feels Wrong

If your combined rating seems lower than it should be , or if you believe an individual condition was rated below its true severity , you have one year from the rating decision date to appeal without losing your effective date. The Appeals Modernization Act gives you three lanes: a Supplemental Claim with new evidence, a Higher-Level Review by a senior adjudicator, or a direct appeal to the Board of Veterans’ Appeals.

Before choosing a lane, it helps to understand exactly what went wrong in the rating decision. Was the correct diagnostic code applied? Was the severity evaluated under the right criteria? Did the VA miss a condition entirely? The answers determine which appeal path has the best chance of success.

title: VA Duty to Assist Errors: When VA Fails to Develop Your Claim
excerpt: VA must make reasonable efforts to obtain certain evidence and provide examinations when required. Learn how to identify a genuine pre-decisional development error.
body:
VA must make reasonable efforts to obtain certain evidence and provide examinations when required. Learn how to identify a genuine pre-decisional development error. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

What the duty to assist actually requires

VA's duty to assist is a legal obligation, not a promise that every claim will be granted. Under 38 U.S.C. § 5103A and 38 C.F.R. § 3.159, VA generally must make reasonable efforts to obtain relevant records and provide a medical examination or opinion when the statutory criteria are met. The precise duties depend on the type of claim, the information provided, and the record already available.

The important distinction is between evidence VA had a duty to seek and evidence that would merely have been helpful. VA is not required to order an examination in every claim, and a veteran's disagreement with a medical conclusion is not by itself proof of a duty-to-assist error.

Missing service and federal records

Service treatment records, relevant personnel records, and identified federal medical records can establish an in-service event or show symptoms long before a civilian diagnosis. If VA made a decision without adequately pursuing relevant federal records, the development may be deficient. A veteran should identify the unit, installation, approximate dates, treatment facility, or deployment involved.

If records cannot be located, VA has notice obligations. An absence of documentation in an incomplete file should not be treated as conclusive proof that an event never occurred. At the same time, missing records do not automatically establish the claimed event or medical nexus.

Private records and the veteran’s role

VA can help request private treatment records when the veteran identifies the provider and provides required authorization, often on VA Forms 21-4142 and 21-4142a. Incomplete provider information or missing authorization can prevent a request. Keep copies of records yourself where possible, and identify why each provider's records matter.

A private physician's record may document years of symptoms, a diagnosis, or treatment soon after discharge. The value lies in its relevance to the denied element, not simply the number of pages submitted.

Practical takeaway: Before choosing a review option or submitting more evidence, compare the rating decision with the records VA actually considered. The most useful next step addresses the precise missing legal or factual element.

When an examination or medical opinion is required

For an original service-connection claim, the examination threshold considers evidence of current disability or persistent symptoms, evidence establishing a relevant service event, an indication the condition may be associated with service, and whether the file otherwise contains sufficient medical evidence. This is not the same as already proving the claim. Credible lay evidence can matter, depending on the facts.

If an exam is provided, adequacy matters. An opinion that ignores material medical history, relies on an inaccurate factual premise, or supplies no understandable reasoning may require correction. But a negative opinion is not automatically inadequate merely because it is unfavorable.

What happens after an HLR finds a pre-decisional error

A Higher-Level Review can identify a duty-to-assist error that existed before the decision being reviewed. VA typically closes the HLR issue and establishes a separate process to obtain the missing evidence, such as records or a new examination, before issuing a new decision. This is a development correction, not an award of benefits.

The veteran should attend requested examinations, verify contact information, and monitor for notices. A correction can still result in a denial if the completed evidence does not support entitlement.

How to articulate the error precisely

A useful argument names the missing action and why the record triggered it: 'The service records documented repeated ankle complaints, the claim identified ongoing ankle pain, and VA denied without obtaining a medical examination or opinion.' Compare that with a vague statement that 'VA failed its duty to assist.' Specificity gives the reviewer a concrete record-based issue to resolve.

Review the decision date carefully. Evidence created after that decision ordinarily cannot establish that VA committed a pre-decisional duty-to-assist error by failing to consider it. Later evidence may instead support a Supplemental Claim.

Questions to ask before you file

  • What exactly did VA concede in its favorable findings, and what element remains disputed?
  • Which evidence was already in the record when VA made the decision?
  • Is the issue a legal or factual mistake, missing development, or a genuine lack of supporting evidence?
  • What is the date of the decision notice, and which review deadline applies?
  • Would the proposed evidence answer the specific reason VA gave for its decision?

Official rules and further reading

The primary authorities and VA guidance below provide a starting point. Regulations and interpretations can change, and the law applicable to an older decision may differ from the law currently in effect.

title: VA Effective Date Errors: How to Challenge Incorrect Back Pay
excerpt: Learn how VA effective dates work, common retroactive-pay errors, continuous pursuit, and when earlier effective dates may be available.
body:
Winning service connection or an increased rating does not end the analysis. The effective date controls when entitlement begins and can determine substantial retroactive compensation. An incorrect date may arise from a missed filing, an overlooked appeal, or a misapplied exception.

The General Rule Is Not the Whole Story

Under 38 C.F.R. § 3.400, effective dates generally depend on the type of claim and the later of the date VA received the claim or the date entitlement arose, subject to many exceptions. A veteran’s diagnosis date is not automatically the effective date, and the date of the C&P examination is not necessarily the date entitlement first arose.

For increased-rating claims, a special one-year lookback may apply when an increase was factually ascertainable within the relevant period. Intent-to-file rules can also matter in qualifying circumstances.

Continuous Pursuit Can Preserve an Earlier Date

Under the modern review system, timely and properly pursued review options can preserve an effective-date chain. A veteran who files a qualifying review request within the applicable period may avoid losing the original date solely because VA initially denied the claim.

A late or incorrectly filed review request can break continuous pursuit. The sequence of notices, forms, and receipt dates matters.

New Service Records Can Trigger a Different Rule

38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c) addresses certain relevant official service department records that existed but were not associated with the file when VA first decided a claim. Qualifying records can require reconsideration, and an award based all or in part on them may implicate an earlier effective date.

This is not a blanket rule for every newly uploaded record. The type of record, relevance, exceptions, and basis of the eventual award must be examined carefully.

CUE Is Not a Substitute for Every Missed Appeal

Clear and unmistakable error is a demanding collateral challenge to a final decision. It generally requires identifying an undebatable error of fact or law that would have manifestly changed the outcome based on the law and record applicable to the earlier decision.

A disagreement over how VA weighed evidence usually is not enough. Before alleging CUE, examine whether continuous pursuit, newly associated service records, or another effective-date rule offers a more appropriate route.

How to Audit the Effective Date

Create a timeline showing every claim, intent to file, decision, notice, review request, and award. Compare the dates with the decision’s stated legal rationale and any exceptions. Remember that compensation payment commencement rules can affect when money is actually paid.

A useful appeal identifies the precise earlier date requested and the legal and factual reason that date applies, not merely that the veteran has been disabled for years.

What to Do Before Filing or Appealing

An effective-date review is often document-intensive. The claim history can matter as much as the medical records.

Keep the rating decision and notification letter, identify the exact issue under dispute, collect the relevant records, and review the deadline before selecting a review option. Evidence that answers VA’s specific reason for denial is more useful than a stack of unrelated documents.

title: VA GERD Ratings After the 2024 Digestive-System Changes
excerpt: GERD received its own diagnostic code in 2024. Learn why the current criteria focus on esophageal stricture and why older rating decisions need careful review.
body:
GERD received its own diagnostic code in 2024. Learn why the current criteria focus on esophageal stricture and why older rating decisions need careful review. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

Why the date of the rating criteria matters

VA revised the digestive-system rating schedule effective May 19, 2024. GERD now has its own Diagnostic Code 7206 under 38 C.F.R. § 4.114. Older GERD awards and appeals may involve the pre-amendment schedule, often by analogy to hiatal hernia under former Diagnostic Code 7346. The applicable criteria depend on the claim's procedural history and the rules governing regulatory changes.

It is inaccurate to tell every veteran that heartburn, regurgitation, or medication automatically qualifies for a particular current GERD percentage. The revised criteria use a different framework.

What current Diagnostic Code 7206 focuses on

The current GERD criteria evaluate documented esophageal stricture, including dysphagia, and the treatment needed to address it. The schedule distinguishes levels involving daily symptoms controlled by medication, dilation or stenting, recurrent or refractory strictures, and more serious interventions. The exact rating requires applying the full regulatory text to the clinical record.

An upper endoscopy, barium swallow, specialist evaluation, or documented intervention may be important depending on the claimed severity. Symptoms alone should be described accurately, but they are not a substitute for the specific findings required by the current code.

GERD symptoms still matter clinically

Reflux, burning pain, sour regurgitation, nighttime choking, difficulty swallowing, and weight or nutrition changes should be reported to treating clinicians. They help explain the course of the condition and may lead to evaluation for esophageal complications. However, rating eligibility and medical treatment decisions are different questions.

Do not stop prescribed treatment to try to demonstrate worse symptoms at a C&P examination. Document what happens despite treatment, including any breakthrough symptoms or complications.

Practical takeaway: Before choosing a review option or submitting more evidence, compare the rating decision with the records VA actually considered. The most useful next step addresses the precise missing legal or factual element.

Older claims and the former analogy to hiatal hernia

Before the amendment, GERD was often evaluated by analogy under former Diagnostic Code 7346, which considered combinations of symptoms and impairment of health. For a claim spanning the regulatory change, the effective date and applicable version of the schedule can affect the analysis. The newer criteria should not simply be projected backward to periods before their effective date.

A review should identify the exact period at issue, the rating decision date, and which version of the criteria VA applied. An appeal about a 2022 rating can raise different questions from a new claim filed in 2026.

Evidence for an accurate evaluation

Gather gastroenterology notes, diagnostic studies, medication history, swallowing complaints, documented strictures, dilation or stenting records, and any treatment for complications. Explain how symptoms affect eating, sleeping, and daily activities without assuming those descriptions alone determine the schedular percentage.

Where the records show a serious swallowing problem, a qualified clinician should address its cause rather than automatically attribute every symptom to GERD.

What to do after an unexpected GERD rating

Compare the decision's diagnostic code and cited criteria with the version of 38 C.F.R. § 4.114 applicable to the relevant period. Review whether the examiner obtained the information the code requires. If the decision overlooks relevant records or applies the wrong standard, determine whether timely review, additional evidence, or an increase claim is appropriate.

Because this area changed recently, generic online charts copied from pre-2024 articles can be misleading. Always verify the regulatory version and date.

Questions to ask before you file

  • What exactly did VA concede in its favorable findings, and what element remains disputed?
  • Which evidence was already in the record when VA made the decision?
  • Is the issue a legal or factual mistake, missing development, or a genuine lack of supporting evidence?
  • What is the date of the decision notice, and which review deadline applies?
  • Would the proposed evidence answer the specific reason VA gave for its decision?

title: VA Hearing Loss Ratings: Why a Severe Problem Can Still Be 0%
excerpt: Hearing loss ratings rely heavily on specified audiometric measurements. Learn the test requirements, mechanical rating tables, and evidence that still matters.
body:
Hearing loss ratings rely heavily on specified audiometric measurements. Learn the test requirements, mechanical rating tables, and evidence that still matters. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

Hearing loss ratings use specific tests

VA generally evaluates hearing impairment under 38 C.F.R. §§ 4.85 and 4.86. A qualifying examination for rating purposes includes a controlled speech discrimination test using the Maryland CNC word list and a puretone audiometry test, conducted by a state-licensed audiologist without hearing aids. The specific frequencies and scores feed into rating tables.

A general statement that a veteran has 'moderate' or 'severe' hearing loss does not directly translate to a compensation percentage. Audiometric values, not the descriptive adjective, control the standard calculation.

Why a 0% rating can be correct

The rating tables assign Roman numeral hearing levels to each ear and combine them to determine the percentage. A veteran can have a service-connected hearing loss disability and still receive a noncompensable 0% evaluation under those tables. That result can feel disconnected from the everyday difficulty of understanding speech in crowds or on the telephone.

The distinction matters: service connection recognizes that the disability is related to service, while the percentage measures severity under VA's prescribed schedule.

Exceptional patterns of hearing impairment

Section 4.86 provides special rules for certain exceptional puretone patterns. For example, specified high thresholds at each of the four tested frequencies or a particular combination at 1,000 and 2,000 Hertz can trigger an alternate table method. Not every severe audiogram qualifies, so review the actual values.

A hearing-loss appeal should check whether the examiner used the proper test and whether the rater correctly applied the exceptional-pattern provisions when they were triggered.

Practical takeaway: Before choosing a review option or submitting more evidence, compare the rating decision with the records VA actually considered. The most useful next step addresses the precise missing legal or factual element.

Functional effects still belong in the record

An audiologist should describe the functional effects of hearing impairment. Veterans can explain difficulty understanding instructions, communicating at work, participating in family conversations, or detecting alarms. Those descriptions help present the full disability picture, even though the ordinary schedular percentage is generally derived mechanically from the audiometric tables.

Keep records of hearing aids, audiology visits, and work accommodations. Avoid assuming that use of hearing aids automatically produces a particular rating.

Hearing loss and tinnitus are different issues

Tinnitus and hearing loss may be separately claimed when supported by the evidence, but they are distinct disabilities with different rating criteria. A veteran can have substantial tinnitus with a 0% hearing-loss evaluation, or vice versa. Do not assume that one award establishes the other.

Noise exposure history, service records, onset statements, and competent medical evidence can all matter when service connection itself is disputed.

When to seek an increased rating or appeal

If hearing has worsened, updated qualifying audiometry may support an increase claim. If a recent decision misapplied a test result or overlooked exceptional-pattern rules, a timely review may be appropriate. A private audiogram may be useful, but its testing protocol must be assessed before assuming it can be used directly for the rating tables.

Review both ears' values and the speech discrimination method rather than relying on a single headline number or hearing-aid prescription.

  • Which evidence was already in the record when VA made the decision?

title: VA Migraine Ratings: What Supports a 30% or 50% Evaluation?
excerpt: The migraine schedule looks at characteristic prostrating attacks and their economic impact. Learn how to document attacks without relying on vague labels.
body:
The migraine schedule looks at characteristic prostrating attacks and their economic impact. Learn how to document attacks without relying on vague labels. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

The migraine diagnostic code

VA generally evaluates migraine headaches under Diagnostic Code 8100 in 38 C.F.R. § 4.124a. The schedule provides 0%, 10%, 30%, and 50% levels based on the pattern of characteristic prostrating attacks and, at the maximum level, severe economic inadaptability. The term 'prostrating' is central and should be supported by a description of what an attack actually does.

A headache diagnosis or a prescription alone does not establish the rating. The frequency, duration, functional severity, and resulting disruption must be developed.

Understanding the 30% criterion

The 30% criterion addresses characteristic prostrating attacks occurring on average once a month over the last several months. An attack that requires stopping activity, lying down, withdrawing from light and noise, or being unable to perform ordinary tasks may be relevant, depending on the full evidence. The key is not simply how much it hurts on a scale from one to ten.

If attacks vary, explain the number of episodes that actually prevent normal functioning, not just the number of days with any head pain.

What makes the 50% criterion different

The maximum 50% evaluation contemplates very frequent, completely prostrating and prolonged attacks productive of severe economic inadaptability. That language has several components: frequency, degree of incapacity, duration, and economic effect. Severe economic inadaptability does not necessarily require proof that the veteran is entirely unemployed.

Document canceled work shifts, reduced hours, lost productivity, disciplinary warnings, depleted leave, and inability to sustain regular tasks. Evidence should explain the relationship between the attacks and economic disruption, rather than assuming that a certain number of headaches automatically meets 50%.

Practical takeaway: Before choosing a review option or submitting more evidence, compare the rating decision with the records VA actually considered. The most useful next step addresses the precise missing legal or factual element.

Keep a useful headache log

A log should record the date, start and end time, symptoms, medications, whether the attack required lying down, missed activities, and whether the veteran could work. Track several months rather than a handful of especially bad days. Contemporaneous records are particularly useful when an examination occurs on a symptom-free day.

Treatment notes can help corroborate severity, but a veteran's competent observations of recurring attacks also matter. Keep descriptions specific and consistent.

Secondary service connection and migraine claims

Migraines may be claimed directly or as secondary to another service-connected disability when the medical evidence supports causation or aggravation. A nexus opinion should address the veteran's medical history, relevant literature when appropriate, and competing causes. Temporal association alone does not prove causation.

Separate the service-connection question from the rating question: a veteran can prove that migraines are service connected and still need stronger evidence to establish the correct percentage.

Common rating mistakes

VA may focus on headache frequency without evaluating whether attacks are prostrating, or acknowledge missed work without analyzing severe economic inadaptability. The reverse also occurs: a claimant may describe severe pain but provide little information about the actual inability to function. The decision should be evaluated against each element of the diagnostic code.

If the veteran's condition has worsened since the last decision, an increase claim may be appropriate. If the earlier decision misread evidence already before VA, timely review may be the better route.

title: VA PTSD Ratings: Understanding 30%, 50%, 70%, and 100%
excerpt: PTSD ratings turn on occupational and social impairment, not simply a symptom checklist. Understand the levels and how to document functional effects.
body:
PTSD ratings turn on occupational and social impairment, not simply a symptom checklist. Understand the levels and how to document functional effects. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

The general rating formula governs PTSD

PTSD is evaluated under the General Rating Formula for Mental Disorders in 38 C.F.R. § 4.130, generally using Diagnostic Code 9411. The criteria focus on the level of occupational and social impairment. Examples of symptoms appear at each percentage, but the inquiry is not a mechanical count of symptoms. Frequency, severity, duration, and functional impact matter.

A veteran does not need to display every example listed at a rating level. Conversely, mentioning one symptom associated with a higher percentage does not automatically establish that rating. VA should evaluate the overall disability picture.

What 30% and 50% generally describe

A 30% evaluation contemplates occupational and social impairment with occasional decrease in work efficiency and intermittent inability to perform occupational tasks, while the person generally functions satisfactorily. A 50% evaluation describes reduced reliability and productivity, with examples such as difficulty maintaining effective work and social relationships, disturbances of motivation and mood, and certain memory or judgment problems.

For evidence, distinguish a bad day from a persistent pattern. Work attendance records, documented conflicts, withdrawal from relationships, and treatment notes can show whether symptoms cause occasional disruption or more sustained reduced reliability.

Why 70% is not simply “severe PTSD”

A 70% evaluation involves deficiencies in most areas, such as work, school, family relations, judgment, thinking, or mood. Examples include difficulty adapting to stressful circumstances, inability to establish and maintain effective relationships, impaired impulse control, or suicidal ideation. VA must consider the actual functional effects and should not reduce the analysis to a label like 'moderate' or 'severe.'

Suicidal ideation is an important symptom to report accurately to treating professionals and examiners. The rating question remains the overall impairment, and any immediate safety concern should be addressed as a health priority, not treated merely as claims evidence.

Practical takeaway: Before choosing a review option or submitting more evidence, compare the rating decision with the records VA actually considered. The most useful next step addresses the precise missing legal or factual element.

The demanding 100% standard

The 100% schedular criterion is total occupational and social impairment. Examples include gross impairment in thought processes or communication, persistent danger of hurting self or others, and profound memory or orientation problems. A veteran does not necessarily have to exhibit each example, but the total-impairment standard is substantial.

A veteran who cannot sustain substantially gainful employment due to service-connected disabilities may also need to consider TDIU, which is a different benefit theory from a 100% schedular PTSD rating.

How to document impairment without exaggeration

Describe what happens in ordinary life: missed shifts, inability to complete tasks, isolation, panic episodes, irritability, concentration failures, or breakdown of relationships. Give timeframes and examples. Treatment records, statements from family, and employment history can corroborate the pattern. Consistency is more persuasive than dramatic language.

At a C&P examination, explain the usual severity and frequency of symptoms rather than describing only how you feel on that particular day. If symptoms fluctuate, explain both the better and worse periods.

When an appeal or increase is appropriate

If VA acknowledged symptoms but assigned a percentage inconsistent with documented impairment, review the examination and reasons for decision. An increase claim is generally used when an already service-connected disability worsens. A timely review of a recent rating decision is a different procedural question. Choose the route that matches the issue and available evidence.

Mental-health diagnoses generally are not separately rated for the same overlapping psychiatric manifestations. Focus on the total service-connected psychiatric impairment rather than multiplying diagnostic labels.

  • Which evidence was already in the record when VA made the decision?

title: Secondary Service Connection: Connecting a New Condition to a VA Disability
excerpt: A disability can qualify when a service-connected condition causes or aggravates it. Learn the evidence VA evaluates under 38 C.F.R. § 3.310.
body:
A disability can qualify when a service-connected condition causes or aggravates it. Learn the evidence VA evaluates under 38 C.F.R. § 3.310. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

The two paths: causation and aggravation

Secondary service connection recognizes that a disability can result from another condition VA has already service connected. Under 38 C.F.R. § 3.310, the question may be whether the primary disability caused the new condition or whether it aggravated the new condition beyond its natural progression. Those are distinct medical theories and should not be treated as interchangeable.

For example, a service-connected orthopedic injury might alter gait and contribute to another joint problem. A clinician should explain the mechanism and the particular veteran's medical history rather than simply assert that one diagnosis commonly accompanies another.

The evidence you need

The record ordinarily must establish a current secondary disability, an already service-connected primary condition, and a competent link between them. The link may come from medical literature, clinical records, a reasoned medical opinion, or a combination of evidence. Medical articles alone seldom establish the relationship in an individual case without explanation of how the research applies.

Lay statements can establish observable symptoms, onset, and changes in function. They usually cannot replace a specialized medical explanation when causation involves complex physiology.

Aggravation is not the same as causation

A condition can predate the primary disability and still be aggravated by it. Under the aggravation provisions of § 3.310, VA considers baseline severity and the degree of additional disability attributable to the service-connected condition. Records from before the worsening and during the worsening can be especially useful.

A medical opinion that only answers 'Did PTSD cause sleep apnea?' may leave unanswered whether PTSD-related factors aggravated sleep apnea. The adequacy of an opinion depends on the actual theories raised and facts of the case.

Practical takeaway: Before choosing a review option or submitting more evidence, compare the rating decision with the records VA actually considered. The most useful next step addresses the precise missing legal or factual element.

Common secondary-claim examples

Examples that may warrant individualized medical analysis include radiculopathy associated with a lumbar spine disability, headaches associated with a service-connected neck condition, gastrointestinal effects of medication prescribed for a service-connected disability, and psychiatric consequences of chronic pain. None of these connections is automatic. Diagnoses, mechanisms, alternative causes, and medical chronology matter.

Be wary of online lists promising that a specific diagnosis always produces a secondary award. VA must still determine whether the facts satisfy the legal and medical requirements.

Avoid duplicate compensation

A veteran may have several diagnoses but cannot receive separate ratings for the same manifestations when doing so would constitute pyramiding under 38 C.F.R. § 4.14. On the other hand, distinct neurological, orthopedic, or other manifestations may warrant separate evaluations when the rating schedule permits it. The issue is overlap of symptoms, not simply overlap of diagnoses.

Review both the service-connection theory and the eventual evaluation. Winning secondary service connection does not guarantee a particular percentage.

Building a persuasive submission

Describe the primary service-connected condition, when the secondary symptoms began, how the symptoms changed, what treating clinicians observed, and what other plausible causes exist. Ask a qualified clinician to explain the relationship using case-specific facts and clear reasoning. If VA denied the claim for lack of nexus, obtain evidence addressing that precise deficiency.

Keep track of the date the secondary claim was filed. The effective date for a newly claimed secondary condition is not automatically the same as the effective date of the primary disability.

  • What exactly did VA concede in its favorable findings, and what element remains disputed?
  • Which evidence was already in the record when VA made the decision?
  • Is the issue a legal or factual mistake, missing development, or a genuine lack of supporting evidence?

title: VA Sleep Apnea Ratings: How to Qualify for 50% Disability
excerpt: Sleep apnea VA disability ratings explained: CPAP use, diagnostic evidence, service connection, and what to do if VA assigns the wrong evaluation.
body:
Sleep apnea claims often turn on two different questions: whether the condition is service connected and what percentage VA should assign. A sleep study can establish obstructive sleep apnea, but a diagnosis alone does not establish that military service caused it. Once service connection is established, the rating schedule determines the percentage.

How VA Rates Sleep Apnea Under Diagnostic Code 6847

Under 38 C.F.R. § 4.97, Diagnostic Code 6847, the longstanding rating criteria assign 0 percent for documented sleep-disordered breathing without symptoms, 30 percent for persistent daytime hypersomnolence, 50 percent when the condition requires use of a breathing-assistance device such as a CPAP machine, and 100 percent for specified severe respiratory findings such as chronic respiratory failure with carbon dioxide retention, cor pulmonale, or a required tracheostomy. The applicable version of the regulation and effective date matter. Proposed changes are not automatically current law.

The 50 percent criterion concerns whether a breathing-assistance device is medically required, not whether the veteran likes using it. A prescription, sleep study, treatment notes, and evidence of the provider’s recommendation can be critical. A CPAP prescription does not itself prove service connection.

Service Connection Comes Before the Percentage

A veteran may establish sleep apnea directly, secondarily, or through another legally supported theory. Direct claims often involve symptoms in service, contemporaneous reports of snoring or breathing pauses, later sleep testing, and competent medical evidence addressing the relationship. Secondary claims may involve whether an established service-connected disability caused or aggravated sleep apnea.

VA must evaluate the evidence rather than assume that every diagnosis occurring after service is unrelated. At the same time, the mere fact that two diagnoses coexist does not establish causation.

What Evidence Supports a 50 Percent Evaluation

Relevant evidence may include the diagnostic sleep study, prescription for CPAP or another qualifying breathing-assistance device, sleep clinic notes, and a Disability Benefits Questionnaire addressing treatment requirements. Keep copies of any documentation showing why the device is required.

If VA assigns 30 percent despite records showing a medically required CPAP, compare the rating decision’s factual findings against the evidence and the version of the rating criteria applicable to the claim.

What If VA Denies Service Connection or Assigns 30 Percent

A denial of service connection requires a different response from an underrating. Review the favorable findings, the examiner’s medical reasoning, and the decision’s discussion of the evidence. An appeal may focus on a missing nexus, an inadequate opinion, or overlooked CPAP documentation.

Depending on the decision and evidence, the appropriate review option may be Higher-Level Review, a Supplemental Claim with new and relevant evidence, or a Board appeal. Deadlines can affect the effective date.

Common Questions About CPAP Ratings

Does every CPAP user automatically receive 50 percent? No. The veteran must first establish service connection, and the applicable rating criteria must be satisfied. Does stopping CPAP use necessarily eliminate entitlement? Not automatically. The question is whether the condition requires the device, based on the evidence and governing rules.

Can a veteran receive a 100 percent sleep apnea rating? The schedule provides a 100 percent level, but it requires substantially more severe qualifying findings than ordinary CPAP use.

What to Do Before Filing or Appealing

A rating dispute may be resolved by identifying exactly what VA overlooked: the device requirement, the medical evidence, or the underlying service-connection theory.

Keep the rating decision and notification letter, identify the exact issue under dispute, collect the relevant records, and review the deadline before selecting a review option. Evidence that answers VA’s specific reason for denial is more useful than a stack of unrelated documents.

title: VA TDIU Benefits: How to Qualify for 100% Compensation Without a 100% Rating
excerpt: Understand TDIU eligibility, 38 CFR 4.16 percentage thresholds, employment evidence, and how VA evaluates unemployability.
body:
Total disability based on individual unemployability, or TDIU, can pay compensation at the 100 percent rate even when a veteran’s combined schedular evaluation is below 100 percent. The question is not simply whether the veteran is unemployed. It is whether service-connected disabilities prevent securing or following substantially gainful employment.

The Schedular TDIU Thresholds

Under 38 C.F.R. § 4.16(a), the usual percentage requirements are one service-connected disability rated at least 60 percent, or multiple disabilities with one rated at least 40 percent and a combined rating of at least 70 percent. Certain disabilities may be considered one disability for threshold purposes under the regulation.

Meeting the percentage threshold does not guarantee TDIU. It permits consideration under the schedular pathway; the evidence must still establish unemployability due to service-connected conditions.

What If the Veteran Does Not Meet the Thresholds

Under § 4.16(b), a veteran who does not satisfy the percentage requirements may still warrant extraschedular TDIU consideration when the evidence supports inability to secure and follow substantially gainful employment because of service-connected disabilities.

A below-threshold claim should not be dismissed solely because the combined rating is too low. The record may require referral for extraschedular consideration.

Unemployed Is Not the Same as Unemployable

VA evaluates functional limitations from service-connected conditions, considering education, training, and occupational history. The inquiry can include physical and mental requirements of work, reliability, concentration, attendance, and the ability to perform work tasks.

Age and impairment from non-service-connected conditions are not bases for awarding TDIU. The strongest evidence connects specific service-connected symptoms to occupational limitations.

Can You Work and Receive TDIU

Some employment may be marginal rather than substantially gainful. Protected work environments and earnings below applicable poverty thresholds can raise special issues, but the analysis is fact-specific. A blanket claim that any work automatically disqualifies a veteran is incorrect.

Veterans should accurately report employment and earnings and should not rely on simplistic online rules about how much income is “allowed.”

How to Document the Claim

VA Form 21-8940, employment history, employer information, treatment records, vocational evidence, and statements describing day-to-day occupational limitations may be useful. A persuasive record explains what tasks the veteran cannot reliably perform and why.

If VA denies TDIU, check whether it evaluated all service-connected disabilities together and meaningfully considered the veteran’s work and education history.

What to Do Before Filing or Appealing

TDIU is a vocational and legal determination informed by medical evidence. A carefully developed record connects service-connected limitations to real-world work requirements.

Keep the rating decision and notification letter, identify the exact issue under dispute, collect the relevant records, and review the deadline before selecting a review option. Evidence that answers VA’s specific reason for denial is more useful than a stack of unrelated documents.

We can review the decision, identify potential factual or legal errors, evaluate the evidence, and help determine the appropriate next step. VA-accredited claims agents are not attorneys, and representation does not guarantee a particular outcome.

title: DIC & Survivor Benefits
excerpt: Dependency and Indemnity Compensation provides a monthly, tax-free payment to surviving spouses and dependents when a veteran’s death is service-connected. We help survivors establish the connection and navigate the claims process.
body:
What Is DIC?

Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC) is a monthly, tax-free benefit paid by the VA to surviving spouses, children, and dependent parents of veterans whose deaths were service-connected , or who, at the time of death, were rated totally disabled by the VA for a specified period of time.

DIC is not a one-time payment; it is an ongoing monthly benefit. The base rate for a surviving spouse (without other additions) is set by Congress and adjusted periodically. Additional amounts may be available for dependent children, for Aid and Attendance needs, and in other circumstances.

Who May Qualify

  • Surviving spouse , married to the veteran at the time of death and meeting continuous cohabitation requirements
  • Surviving children , unmarried children under 18, or under 23 if in school, or permanently disabled before age 18
  • Dependent parents , may qualify for a separate benefit based on the veteran’s service-connected death

Paths to Service Connection for the Cause of Death

The central question in most DIC claims is whether the veteran’s death was caused by, or substantially contributed to by, a service-connected or service-connectable condition. This analysis can be complex. The paths include:

  • Direct service connection , the condition that caused death began during or was aggravated by active duty service
  • Secondary service connection , the cause of death was caused or aggravated by an already service-connected condition
  • The 10-year presumption , if the veteran had a continuous total rating for 10 or more years before death, the surviving spouse may be entitled regardless of cause of death
  • The 5-year presumption , a total rating in place for 5 or more years immediately before death, where the condition could not have improved, may also qualify
  • Ratings before death , if the veteran had a claim pending at the time of death, the surviving spouse may be able to substitute for the veteran and continue pursuing that claim

Substitution and Pending Claims

When a veteran dies while a VA claim or appeal is pending, an eligible survivor may apply to substitute for the veteran within one year of the veteran’s death. Substitution allows the survivor to step into the veteran’s shoes and pursue the claim to a final decision , potentially securing retroactive benefits that accrue back to the original filing date.

This is a time-sensitive right. Missing the one-year substitution deadline extinguishes it. If the veteran had a pending claim when they passed, contact us promptly.

title: Discharge Upgrades
excerpt: A less-than-honorable discharge can bar a veteran from VA benefits, employment, and more. We assist veterans in petitioning for character of discharge upgrades before the Discharge Review Boards and Boards for Correction of Military Records.
body:
Why Discharge Character Matters

The character of a veteran’s discharge , Honorable, General (Under Honorable Conditions), Other Than Honorable (OTH), Bad Conduct, or Dishonorable , determines eligibility for most VA benefits. A veteran discharged OTH or worse may be barred from VA health care, disability compensation, education benefits, and other programs that would otherwise be available based on their service.

For some veterans, the discharge characterization reflects circumstances that were shaped by untreated mental health conditions, military sexual trauma, or situations involving systemic error or injustice. The upgrade process exists to address those cases.

Available Forums

  • Discharge Review Board (DRB) , each military branch has a DRB that can review discharges within 15 years of the separation date; can change character of discharge and reason for discharge
  • Board for Correction of Military Records (BCMR) / Board for Correction of Naval Records (BCNR) , available for any discharge, with no time limit; broader authority to correct records and grant relief on grounds of error or injustice
  • Special Discharge Review Programs (SDRP) , certain programs exist specifically for veterans whose discharges were influenced by PTSD, MST, or TBI, or whose cases involve particular era-specific injustices

Grounds for Upgrade

The boards consider whether the discharge was proper (no procedural error) and equitable (fair given all the facts). Strong grounds for an upgrade often include:

  • PTSD, MST, or other mental health conditions that were undiagnosed or untreated at the time of the misconduct underlying the discharge
  • Brain injury or substance abuse disorder directly related to service
  • Systemic injustice or patterns of discrimination that influenced the discharge
  • Evidence that the punishment was disproportionate to the conduct at issue
  • Strong post-service record of rehabilitation, community contribution, or subsequent honorable service

Our Approach to Discharge Upgrade Petitions

We begin with a thorough review of your DD214, service records, and separation documents to understand what happened and why. We then analyze which forum and which theory of relief gives the strongest path to an upgrade. The petition itself is built around a detailed personal statement, corroborating lay statements, medical or mental health evidence, and a legal argument that ties the evidence to the standard the board applies.

Discharge review petitions are not casual filings. A well-built submission significantly improves the odds of success. We take the time to do it right.

title: Correcting Military Records
excerpt: Errors in your DD214 or military service records can affect VA eligibility, employment, and more. We assist veterans in identifying errors and pursuing corrections through the appropriate administrative channels.
body:
Why Military Records Matter

Your DD-214 (Certificate of Release or Discharge from Active Duty) is one of the most important documents you will have after military service. It establishes your service history, character of discharge, awards, occupational specialty, and more. Errors on the DD-214 , or in your underlying service records , can affect VA benefit eligibility, civil service preference, state veterans’ benefits, and employment.

Errors range from simple clerical mistakes (wrong dates, misspelled names, omitted awards) to substantive errors that mischaracterize service or exclude periods of active duty. The correction process depends on the nature and age of the error, and which military branch is involved.

Common Corrections We Assist With

  • Incorrect character of discharge or reason for discharge
  • Missing or incorrect service dates, component, or occupational specialty code
  • Omitted awards, decorations, or citations
  • Incorrect disability rating at separation through IDES/LDES process
  • Missing combat service designations or foreign service entries
  • Errors in narrative reason for separation that affect benefit eligibility
  • Upgrades to general or honorable discharge (overlaps with discharge upgrade petitions)

Correction Forums

The primary forum for correcting military records is the Board for Correction of Military Records (BCMR) for Army, Air Force, Space Force, and Coast Guard veterans, and the Board for Correction of Naval Records (BCNR) for Navy and Marine Corps veterans. These boards have broad authority to correct any military record when necessary to correct an error or remove an injustice.

For clerical errors that have no dispute about the underlying facts, a simpler request to the National Personnel Records Center (NPRC) or the relevant branch may suffice. We assess which avenue is most appropriate for your situation before investing time in the more extensive BCMR/BCNR petition process.

Relationship to VA Claims

Sometimes a military record correction and a VA claim proceed in parallel , or a favorable BCMR/BCNR decision creates retroactive VA entitlement. For example, if the BCMR corrects a record to show that a veteran was medically retired rather than administratively separated, this creates a basis for VA disability compensation dating to the original separation. We consider these downstream effects when advising on whether and how to pursue a record correction.

title: TDIU / Unemployability
excerpt: When service-connected disabilities prevent you from holding substantially gainful employment, VA can pay you at the 100% rate even if your combined rating is below 100%. We build TDIU claims grounded in vocational and medical evidence.
body:
What Is TDIU?

Total Disability based on Individual Unemployability (TDIU) is a VA benefit that allows a veteran to receive compensation at the 100% rate even if their combined disability rating does not reach 100%. It is available when service-connected disabilities alone prevent the veteran from securing or maintaining substantially gainful employment , that is, work paying above the poverty threshold.

TDIU is one of the most significant benefits the VA offers. The difference between, say, a 70% combined rating and a 100% rating can mean several hundred dollars per month in additional compensation. For veterans who are genuinely unable to work because of their service-connected conditions, TDIU is often the correct and deserved outcome.

Eligibility Requirements

There are two paths to TDIU eligibility under the VA's schedular criteria:

  • Single disability at 60% or higher , one service-connected disability rated at 60% or more
  • Multiple disabilities at 70% combined , combined rating of 70% or higher, with at least one disability rated at 40% or more

Even if a veteran does not meet these thresholds, TDIU may still be granted on an extraschedular basis if the case is referred to the Director of Compensation and it is found that the veteran's disabilities render them unemployable. This is a narrower path but an important one for veterans whose situations do not fit neatly into the standard criteria.

What We Look At

A successful TDIU claim requires demonstrating two things: that the veteran's disabilities meet the rating threshold, and that those disabilities , not age, not unrelated conditions , are what prevent employment. We examine:

  • Current combined and individual disability ratings and whether increases are warranted before filing TDIU
  • Employment history and the nature of jobs held after service
  • Medical documentation of functional limitations directly tied to service-connected conditions
  • Lay statements from the veteran, family, and former employers or coworkers
  • Whether a VA vocational rehabilitation determination exists and how it bears on the claim
  • Marginal employment situations that do not constitute substantial gainful employment

Protecting an Existing TDIU Grant

If you are already receiving TDIU, the VA can propose to reduce or terminate it based on improvement in your condition or a finding that you have returned to substantially gainful employment. We also assist veterans in responding to proposed reductions and in protecting awards that have been in place for an extended period, which are subject to stricter procedural protections before they can be reduced.

title: VA Disability Claims
excerpt: Structured representation for initial claims, rating increases, secondary conditions, and AMA appeals , built around disciplined evidence and sound entitlement theory.
body:
What Are VA Disability Claims?

A VA disability claim asks the Department of Veterans Affairs to recognize that a condition was caused or aggravated by military service and assign a disability rating , expressed as a percentage from 0% to 100% , that determines your monthly compensation. The combined rating drives the payment amount, and getting each condition properly rated matters enormously.

Claims can be filed for conditions that arose during service, were aggravated beyond their natural progression by service, or were caused by an already service-connected condition (secondary service connection). Presumptive conditions , those the VA automatically presumes are service-connected under certain circumstances , add another avenue that is often overlooked.

Types of Claims We Handle

  • Initial claims for veterans who have never filed or whose earlier claims were denied
  • Supplemental claims with new and relevant evidence to reopen prior denials
  • Increased rating claims when an existing condition has worsened
  • Secondary service connection for conditions caused or aggravated by a service-connected disability
  • Presumptive conditions, including those covered under the PACT Act for toxic exposure
  • Claims for Individual Unemployability (TDIU) when disabilities prevent substantial gainful employment
  • AMA appeals , Higher-Level Reviews and Board of Veterans' Appeals appeals under the new appeals system

Our Approach

Every claim starts with a thorough review of your service records, medical records, and any prior VA decisions. We identify the conditions that are service-connected or potentially service-connected, map the evidence needed to establish each element of entitlement, and build a submission designed to give the rater everything necessary to grant the claim at the correct rating.

Where evidence gaps exist , private medical opinions, nexus letters, buddy statements, or additional lay evidence , we identify what is needed and work with you to obtain it. We do not file claims speculatively; we file claims that are supported by theory and evidence.

The AMA Appeals Process

If the VA denies your claim or assigns a rating you believe is incorrect, you have one year from the decision date to choose an appeal lane under the Appeals Modernization Act:

  • Supplemental Claim: Submit new and relevant evidence for re-adjudication
  • Higher-Level Review: Request de novo review by a senior claims adjudicator , no new evidence, but errors in the prior decision can be corrected
  • Board of Veterans' Appeals: Direct appeal to a Veterans Law Judge, with or without a hearing, and with or without new evidence (Evidence Submission lane)

Choosing the right lane depends on what went wrong in the original decision. We analyze the rating decision, identify the specific error or missing evidence, and recommend the lane that gives the strongest path to a grant.
